products.body_html:
Red without the bulk, in sterile form. Ludwigia brevipes grows fine needle-like leaves in a bushier arrangement than its close relative Ludwigia arcuata, developing intense orange-red under strong light. This is the Vitro Culture® format — many small plantlets per cup, free of snails and algae.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Needle Leaf Repens
  • Scientific name — Ludwigia brevipes
  • Also known as — Long Beach Primrose Willow, Ludwigia Narrow Leaf, Ludwigia Needle Leaf
  • Origin — Eastern United States
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 in
  • Mature height — 4–10 in

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Light intensity sets how red it goes
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient substrate or root tabs, plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower's Notes

  • Bushier than arcuata, and that is the difference. The two are constantly confused — same fine leaves, same orange-red. Brevipes carries denser foliage per stem, so it fills a midground where arcuata reads as a finer haze.

products.title: Selaginella Kraussiana Mini
products.body_html:
A moss-like carpet that isn't a moss. Selaginella kraussiana 'Mini' is a compact spikemoss forming dense mats of tiny fern-like leaves — fast spreading, fine textured, and built for humid enclosures rather than aquariums.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose fresh-cut plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 6 individual stems without root
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 6 stems without root bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 6 stems without root potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Mini Spikemoss, Mini Clubmoss, Mini Club Moss
  • Scientific name — Selaginella kraussiana 'Mini'
  • True aquatic — No. Terrestrial creeping plant; not suitable for full submersion
  • Placement — Terrarium, vivarium or paludarium foreground, above the waterline
  • Growth habit — Non-Aquatic. Creeping, fast spreading

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner in a humid enclosure
  • Light — Medium to high, avoiding direct intense sunlight
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Humidity — High. Thrives in enclosed tropical setups
  • Substrate — Required. A nutrient substrate sustains growth and colour
  • Propagation — Division or stem cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • It is not an aquarium plant. Kraussiana grows above the waterline in terrariums, vivariums and paludariums. Fully submerged it dies — the moss-like look tempts people into planting it in tanks, and it does not survive there.
  • It spreads fast for a plant this fine. Gaps close quickly into a continuous carpet, which makes it far more practical as terrarium ground cover than true mosses.
  • Keep humidity high and the substrate damp. It is more forgiving than S. erythropus, but still declines quickly in dry air.
  • Good microhabitat for small reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates — dense enough to shelter in, low enough to see over.
  • Divide it to propagate. Any rooted section re-establishes readily.

Notes

  • Pictures are a sample representation; actual plants may vary in size and colour depending on growing conditions. Unless specified, we do not guarantee plants will be pest-free, pesticide-free, or grown in submerged form.
  • Please do not release Selaginella kraussiana 'Mini' or any plants into natural waterways or wild habitats. Always dispose of trimmings responsibly.

products.title: Vallisneria spiralis 'Leopard'
products.body_html:
Want a background plant with markings rather than plain green? Vallisneria spiralis 'Leopard' carries dark spotting scattered along its ribbon leaves — the same easy, fast-spreading Val, with a pattern almost nothing else in a planted tank offers.

What You’ll Receive

  • Bare-root plants | Approx. 2–3 loose plants
  • Bunched plants | Approx. 2–3 plants bundled with foam and lead weight
  • Potted plants | Approx. 2–3 plants in a net pot with rock wool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Leopard Vallisneria, also known as Spotted Val
  • Scientific name — Vallisneria spiralis 'Leopard'
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is widespread
  • Placement — Background, or back and side corners
  • Shipped size — Approx. 2-3 plants, roughly 5-10 in
  • Mature height — 10–20 in
  • Suits — 20 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. The spotting darkens under stronger light
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–8.0. Tolerates hard, alkaline water well
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic. Cannot be grown emersed
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • The spots need light to show. In a dim tank Leopard Val grows perfectly well but reads as ordinary green Vallisneria. If you bought it for the pattern, put it where light reaches.
  • Plant the crown at the substrate line, never below it. A buried crown rots — the usual reason a new Val fails in the first fortnight.
  • Feed at the roots. In inert gravel it survives but barely spreads; root tabs are what turn three plants into a stand.
  • Don't trim the tops to control height. Cut Val leaves brown at the cut and stay that way — remove whole leaves at the base instead.
  • Runners travel fast. Pull unwanted plantlets by hand rather than cutting, and expect to thin it every month or two once established.

products.title: Red Root Floater
products.body_html:
Floats at the surface on round, coin-sized leaves trailing crimson roots into the water column. Given strong light the leaf undersides and margins turn deep red as well, which is the reason most people buy it.

What You’ll Receive

A small portion (approximately 2” × 2”) of healthy Red Root Floater containing approximately 6–8 plants.

Each plant includes multiple leaves, forming small clusters ready to grow and spread on the water surface.

Plants are carefully harvested and packed to ensure they arrive fresh and ready to add directly to your aquarium or pond.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Red Root Floater
  • Scientific name — Phyllanthus fluitans

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate

  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5

products.title: Hygrophila Pink Chai (Small Size)
products.body_html:
Want neon pink rather than red? Hygrophila lancea 'Pink Chai' holds a genuine hot pink through its narrow elongated leaves, shading to green — a colour no other stem plant in our range produces. This listing is the young, miniature size.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pink Chai
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila lancea 'Pink Chai'
  • Also known as — Hygrophila sp. 'Chai', Hygrophila sp. 'Pink Chai', Hygrophila Pink Lady

products.title: Dracaena sanderiana 'Variegatus' – Variegated Lucky Bamboo
products.body_html:
🎋 Dracaena sanderiana 'Variegatus' – Variegated Lucky Bamboo

Dracaena sanderiana 'Variegatus', commonly known as Variegated Lucky Bamboo, is an elegant and low-maintenance plant that brings a touch of serenity and natural beauty to any space. Despite its common name, it’s not a true bamboo but a resilient species from the Dracaena family, prized for its striking green leaves edged with creamy white or yellow variegation.

Perfect for both aquariums and decorative indoor arrangements, this plant thrives in water or moist soil, making it ideal for homes, offices, or feng shui displays.

Important: only the stem may sit in water. The leaves are not aquatic and will rot if kept submerged — position the plant so the foliage grows above the waterline.

🌟 Key Features

  • Scientific Name: Dracaena sanderiana 'Variegatus'

  • Common Name: Variegated Lucky Bamboo

  • Appearance: Elegant green stalks with glossy leaves featuring creamy white margins

  • Versatile Growth: Can be grown in water, hydroponic setups, or soil

  • True aquatic: No — stem tolerates submersion, leaves must stay above water

  • Symbolism: Represents luck, prosperity, and positive energy in feng shui culture

  • Low Maintenance: Ideal for beginners and busy plant owners

🌱 Growth & Care

  • Lighting: Prefers bright, indirect light but tolerates low-light conditions

  • Watering: Keep roots submerged in clean, chlorine-free water; change weekly

  • Temperature: Thrives in 65–90°F (18–32°C)

  • Humidity: Moderate to high humidity preferred

  • Substrate: Can grow in soil, pebbles, or water with proper support

  • Fertilization: Use a mild liquid fertilizer monthly during growing season

🖼️ Display Ideas

  • Perfect for modern home decor, office desks, or zen garden arrangements

  • Combine multiple stems in glass vases or decorative pots for a lush, elegant look

  • Ideal for feng shui placement to invite harmony and prosperity

📦 What You’ll Receive

Sold as fresh-cut, unrooted individual plants:
1 Plant: Approximately 10+ inches tall, ready for water or soil placement.

⚠️ Disclaimer

This plant is shipped fresh-cut and unrooted. Upon arrival, place the stem in clean, chlorine-free water to encourage root development. Avoid direct sunlight to prevent leaf burn.

products.title: Lobelia Cardinalis Wavy
products.body_html:
The same plant, crimped. Lobelia cardinalis 'Wavy' carries the leaf size of ordinary Cardinal Plant but with curled, ruffled edges and a denser, bushier habit — a texture difference you notice immediately in a group planting. It is a recent selection and still uncommon in the trade.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose fresh-cut plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 3 individual, loose-cut stems without root
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 3 stems without root bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 3 stems without root potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Wavy Lobelia Cardinalis
  • Scientific name — Lobelia cardinalis 'Wavy'
  • Also known as — Wavy Cardinal Plant
  • Origin — Cultivated selection; the species is native to the Americas
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Shipped size — Approx. 3 emersed-grown stems, no roots
  • Mature height — 2–6 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high. Stronger light keeps it compact and bushy
  • CO₂ — Not required. It grows denser and faster with it
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5

Grower's Notes

  • The colour you see on arrival is not the colour you keep. We grow it emersed, where leaf tops are green and the undersides flush red-purple. Submerged it settles to lush green and the wavy edges become the feature instead. Neither state is wrong — it is the plant converting.
  • Trim the main shoot early. Cutting it triggers multiple side shoots, and that is what produces the dense ruffled cushion this selection is bought for. Left untopped it grows as a single stem and the effect is lost.
  • It is slow. That makes it well behaved in a small tank and a poor choice if you want quick coverage.
  • Feed at the roots. Lobelia roots strongly and stays short and pale in inert gravel.
  • A single well-branched plant works as a foreground focal point; several planted together suit a Dutch-style row. Compare with the much larger Lobelia sp. 'Giant' if you need height instead.

products.title: Aciotis Acuminifolia Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Colour on the underside, not the top. Aciotis acuminifolia grows deep green leaves backed with reddish-purple — so the plant reads green from above and flushes violet wherever a leaf turns or catches light from below. It is rare in the hobby, from tropical South America, and unrelated to anything else in a typical planted tank.

What You’ll Receive

Healthy, lab-grown Aciotis acuminifolia cultivated by Aquarium Plants Factory® in sterile Vitro Culture® conditions. Each 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag contains multiple healthy plantlets ready for planting and acclimation.

  • 1 Bag
  • 5 Bags
  • 10 Bags

  • Common name — Aciotis
  • Scientific name — Aciotis acuminifolia
  • Also known as — Purple-backed Aciotis

products.title: Flame Moss
products.body_html:
Every other moss sprawls sideways — Flame Moss grows up. Its fronds twist vertically in curling, flame-like columns, giving a planted tank a sense of movement and height that no other moss can produce.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a small loose portion, approx. 2" x 2" in size
  • Perfect to attached to driftwood, rock, or stone

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Flame Moss
  • Scientific name — Taxiphyllum sp. 'Flame'
  • Also sold as — Vesicularia sp. 'Flame'
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 2–4 in of upright growth
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light brings algae it grows too slowly to shed
  • CO₂ — Not required! Tighter and faster with it, perfectly happy without
  • Water — 70–82°F · pH 5.0–8.0, one of the widest ranges of any plant
  • Feeding — Water column
  • Propagation — Fragmentation; divide and reattach small sections

Grower’s Notes

  • Tie it in a thin, flat layer and let it rise on its own. The vertical growth is what you are paying for, and a thick clump smothers that shape before it forms.
  • Cooler water gives tighter flames. In warm tanks the fronds loosen and lengthen, losing the twisting column look.
  • Trim the tops rather than the sides. Cutting the tips forces new upright shoots and keeps the flame effect dense.
  • Be patient. It is slow even by moss standards and takes a couple of months to knit onto hardscape — that slowness is why it holds its shape so well.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference. Portion size, density and frond shape vary with temperature and growing conditions.

products.body_html:
Often confused with Limnophila aromatica, and easy to tell apart once you know. Limnophila hippuridoides carries noticeably more than three leaves per whorl, giving a denser, bushier stem — and under strong light the undersides deepen to reddish-purple. Native to the Malay Peninsula.

Grower’s Notes

  • Count the leaves to identify it. L. aromatica carries three or four leaves per whorl; hippuridoides carries more. If you're buying both, label them — once they're growing side by side they are genuinely hard to tell apart.
  • The purple sits on the leaf undersides. Position it where light rakes across the group rather than straight down, or the colour hides.
  • Trim and replant tops. Fast growth plus repeated topping is what builds the dense bushy stand this plant is bought for.

'Belem' grows narrow, toothed leaves on compact bushy stems — shorter and denser than most Limnophila, and sharper in texture than the feathery whorls the genus is known for. It stays green in moderate conditions and shifts toward red and purple under strong light with CO₂. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® (tissue culture) format.

  • Placement — Midground to background

  • Green on arrival is correct. Tissue culture plantlets are grown emersed and come out of the bag plain green. The red and purple develop over several weeks of submerged growth under strong light — judge the plant on its new growth.
  • The serrated edge is what sets it apart. Most Limnophila carry fine feathery whorls; 'Belem' has long narrow leaves with a toothed margin, giving a sharper, more defined texture in a group planting.
  • Without CO₂ it stays green. It will grow perfectly well, but the colour that makes it worth buying needs injection. If you are not running CO₂, pick a plant that colours without it rather than expecting this one to.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Tonkinensis Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Long, narrow, ribbon-like leaves that rise in a loose spiral. Cryptocoryne crispatula var. tonkinensis is one of the tall crispatula forms — a background crypt that gives the vertical movement of Vallisneria without needing CO₂ or strong light. Colour runs green to reddish-brown depending on conditions. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a Tissue Culture Plants with vitamin liquid/gel
  • Packaging May Vary! To be sent in either in vitro bag or cup
  • Bag size: Approx. 4 inches. Yield many small plants
  • Sustainable growth aquarium plants species
  • Tissue Culture Technology | 100% Free from Snail, Algae, Pathogen, and Bacteria plus Extended Shelf Life on all in Vitro Plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Tonkinensis Crypt
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne crispatula var. tonkinensis
  • Also known as — Cryptocoryne tonkinensis
  • Origin — Southeast Asia; slow-moving streams and marshes
  • Placement — Background
  • Mature height — 12-20 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5. Hard water suits it, as it does most Crypts.
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs under the crown.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette; also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower's Notes

  • Plant it in a group, at the back. A single rosette of ribbon leaves is unremarkable. Several planted together where there is some flow give the swaying curtain effect that is the whole reason to choose a crispatula form over a broad-leaved crypt.
  • Give it substrate depth. Twelve to twenty inches of leaf needs a deep, well-fed root run. Two inches of nutrient substrate minimum, or root tabs pushed under each crown.
  • Crypt melt is expected and is not failure. Tissue culture plantlets shed their emersed leaves as they convert to submersed growth. Leave the roots undisturbed — new leaves come from the crown within three to six weeks.
  • Plant the crown at substrate level. Bury the roots and leave the growing point exposed. A buried crown rots from the centre.
  • Compare it with our other tall crypts. Balansae is the same species with wider, hammered leaves; Retrospiralis is shorter and more reddish. All three do the same job at the back of a low-tech tank.

products.title: Samolus Parviflorus Red Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Red that stays put. Samolus parviflorus 'Red' grows low, compact rosettes of rounded leaves that turn pink to deep red submerged — no topping, no replanting, no stems falling over. Easier to place than any red stem plant, and it prefers cooler water than most. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as a Vitro Culture® cup in a sealed 4-inch bag:

  • 4-inch Bag: Contains multiple young plants, ready for propagation and planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Red Samolus, Red Water Pimpernel
  • Scientific name — Samolus parviflorus 'Red'

  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 2–6 in

Care

  • Separate side shoots once each has roots of its own; a couple of plants become a patch over a season.

products.title: Hygrophila Difformis | Bulk Pack
products.body_html:
The fastest way to fill a tank. Hygrophila difformis — Water Wisteria — grows lace-cut fern-like leaves at a pace few plants match, taking up nutrients that would otherwise feed algae. That makes it the standard choice for stabilising a new aquarium, and buying it by the bulk pack is how you get a jungle in weeks rather than months.

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Hygrophila Difformis (Water Wisteria) cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in two bulk sizes:

  • 20 Stems — approximately 20 loose fresh-cut stems without roots
  • 40 Stems — approximately 40 loose fresh-cut stems without roots

These are fresh cuttings grown above water (emersed) and will quickly adapt and produce new submerged growth once planted in your aquarium.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Water Wisteria
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila difformis
  • Also known as — Synnema triflorum
  • Origin — Indian subcontinent
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — 20 or 40 fresh-cut stems, no roots
  • Mature height — 10–20 in
  • Suits — 20 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to high. It adapts across the whole range
  • CO₂ — Not required. It grows faster and denser with it
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5

Grower's Notes

  • Expect the leaf shape to change, and do not panic. Emersed-grown stems arrive with broad, rounded, almost solid leaves. Submerged, the plant produces the deeply cut lace-like foliage it is known for. The first leaves may drop entirely — that is the conversion, not a failure.
  • This is the plant for a new tank. Fast uptake of ammonia and nitrate is exactly what an immature aquarium needs, and a bulk pack gives enough plant mass to make a real difference from week one.
  • Plant stems individually an inch apart rather than in bunches. Bunched, the lower stems shade out and rot where the band sits.
  • Trim and replant the tops. Every cutting roots, so 20 stems become 40 within a couple of months if you keep topping them.
  • It grows fast enough to shade whatever is beneath it. Trim on a schedule rather than when it looks untidy.

Notes

10 Plants: Loose bare-root plants with approximately 4+ leaves per plant

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to moderate
  • CO₂ — Not required

  • Buy coverage, do not wait for it. A single Anubias adds a few leaves a year. Twenty plants spread across a piece of wood look established the day they go in; one plant never will. That is the whole argument for buying in bulk.
  • Pointed leaves break up a wall of green. Massed Anubias can look like one undifferentiated clump. The spear shape of 'Peacock' gives a large planting internal texture without changing the care routine.
  • Space them further apart than looks right. Each rhizome needs water movement around it. Where rhizomes press together, detritus collects and rot starts.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Attach with cotton thread or a spot of gel glue; the roots grip the wood themselves within a couple of months.
  • The leathery leaves are usually left alone by fish, which makes a bulk Anubias planting one of the few that works in a goldfish or cichlid tank.

products.title: Anubias Petite Coin | Bulk Pack

Anubias Petite Coin is a cross between Anubias Barteri Round (Golden Coin) and Anubias Nana 'Petite' — it takes the thick, coin-shaped leaf from one parent and the compact size from the other. No other small Anubias has this leaf shape. This is the bulk listing for aquascapers planting a full hardscape rather than a single accent.

  • Common name — Petite Coin Anubias

  • Parentage — Anubias Barteri Round (Golden Coin) × Anubias Nana 'Petite'
  • Origin — Cultivated hybrid; the genus is native to West and Central Africa

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner

products.title: Water Lettuce
products.body_html:
Want surface cover with real presence? Water Lettuce floats as soft velvety rosettes that genuinely look like small heads of lettuce, trailing long feathery roots beneath. It shades the water, strips nutrients, and gives fry and shrimp somewhere to hide. 

What You’ll Receive

Sold as a small portion of loose, Lettuce rosettes (approximately 1–2 plants, depending on size and season).

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Water Lettuce
  • Scientific name — Pistia stratiotes
  • Placement — Floating
  • Mature size — 2–6 in across
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high. Full sun outdoors
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 70–85°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Calm surface, warm water
  • Substrate — Not required. Feeds entirely from the water column
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic, free floating
  • Propagation — Daughter plants on runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Keep the leaves dry. The velvety upper surface is not built to be wet — constant splash from a spray bar, strong HOB return or a dripping lid will rot the rosettes. Aim outflow below the surface, and leave an air gap under a closed lid.
  • The roots are the point. A dense trailing root curtain is where shrimplets and fry shelter, and where much of the nitrate uptake happens — resist trimming them for looks.
  • Thin it weekly. It multiplies fast by runner and a closed mat shades everything below.
  • It wants warmth and will not survive frost outdoors. In tropical and subtropical climates it spreads rapidly — monitor and maintain responsibly.

Want a smaller version for an aquarium? See Dwarf Water Lettuce, which stays 1–2 in across.

Want to go deeper? Read our guide to the Best Floating Plants for Freshwater Aquariums.

Notes

  • We will NOT ship Water Lettuce (Pistia stratiotes) to the following states or territories due to legal restrictions:
    Alabama (AL), California (CA), Florida (FL), Louisiana (LA), Mississippi (MS), South Carolina (SC), Texas (TX), Wisconsin (WI), Ohio (OH), Maine (ME), Puerto Rico (PR).
  • Water Lettuce is sensitive to frost and should not be used in outdoor settings during freezing temperatures. In tropical and subtropical climates, this plant can spread rapidly. Always monitor and maintain responsibly.
  • Please respect local regulations and do not release this plant into natural waterways.

products.body_html:
Brazilian Pennywort is already one of the easiest stem plants sold. The marbled form keeps that and adds cream and pale green streaking across those round, lily-pad leaves — rare-looking foliage on a plant that grows fast enough to fill space in weeks.

Grower's Notes

  • Variegated does not mean difficult here. Pennywort grows fast enough to carry the loss of chlorophyll without slowing down. It stays a beginner plant — the marbling costs you nothing in difficulty.
  • Solid green stems will appear. Any variegated plant can revert, and green growth is more efficient so it spreads if left. Cut reverted stems out at the base as you spot them.
  • It grows in three directions. Planted it climbs, floated it spreads across the surface, and laid against hardscape it creeps. Decide which you want and trim to enforce it — left alone it does all three at once.
  • Every node roots. Cut anywhere and both halves grow. Four stems become a dense patch within a couple of months with nothing more than scissors.
  • Floating stems shade what is below. The leaves are broad and they cover a surface fast. Keep it trimmed back if there is anything light-hungry underneath.

products.title: Dwarf Hairgrass
products.body_html:
Want a grass lawn underwater? Dwarf Hairgrass spreads by runner into a fine, meadow-like carpet — the classic foreground for Iwagumi and nature-style layouts, and the plant most people picture when they imagine a carpeted tank.

You may know it as Eleocharis parvula. That is the trade name — see the note below.

What You’ll Receive

  • Bare-root Plants | small clump portion, bare-root plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Dwarf Hairgrass
  • Scientific name — Eleocharis pusilla
  • Also known as — Eleocharis parvula (misapplied trade name)
  • Origin — Australia and New Zealand
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Shipped size — Small bare-root clump portion
  • Mature height — 3–6 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Why two scientific names?

Dwarf Hairgrass has been sold as Eleocharis parvula in the aquarium trade for a very long time, and most hobbyists still know it by that name.

Eleocharis parvula is a real species — but it is a brackish water plant, not suited to freshwater aquariums. Almost everything sold in the hobby under that label is in fact Eleocharis pusilla, a freshwater species.

So the plant you receive is Eleocharis pusilla: the same Dwarf Hairgrass you have always bought, correctly named, and genuinely suited to a freshwater tank.

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Light must reach the substrate for it to carpet rather than stretch
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Dry start works well
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Split the clump into many small portions. Divide into groups of a few blades and plant them an inch apart. Runners only travel into open substrate, so a single lump takes months longer to fill a foreground than the same plant spread out.
  • Keeping it alive is easy; carpeting it is not. That gap is why this is rated Intermediate. Survival needs little, but a dense low lawn needs strong light at substrate level and usually CO₂ — without both, expect a thin, stretched meadow.
  • Light reaching the substrate is what decides carpet versus stretch. Shaded hairgrass grows long and thin instead of dense and low.
  • Trim the carpet once established. Cutting it back encourages runner growth rather than height.
  • Expect the emersed blades to melt back after planting. New growth comes from the runners, not the original blades.

Want the shorter version? See Dwarf Hairgrass 'Mini', which stays 1–2 in.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Dwarf Hairgrass Care Guide.

Notes

  • Pictures are not the actual plants you will receive, but a sample representation. Unless specific, we don't guarantee aquatic plants will be free of pests, and pesticides, grow emerged or submerge.

products.title: Water Mimosa
products.body_html:
Want a plant that reacts when you touch it? Water Mimosa folds its delicate fern-like leaflets inward within seconds of being disturbed, then opens again once left alone. It floats on spongy buoyant stems, forming a soft green canopy — and it is the only plant we sell that moves on its own.

What You’ll Receive

Healthy Water Mimosa plants carefully prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®.

Variants available:

2 Plants – Unrooted
Fresh-cut floating plants without roots.

2 Plants – Rooted
Fresh-cut floating plants with visible developing roots.

10 Plants – Unrooted
Bulk portion of fresh-cut floating plants without roots.

10 Plants – Rooted
Bulk portion of fresh-cut floating plants with visible developing roots.

All plants are carefully selected and shipped fresh to ensure healthy arrival.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Water Mimosa, also known as Sensitive Water Mimosa
  • Scientific name — Neptunia oleracea
  • Placement — Floating
  • Mature height — 6–8 in above the surface
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 70–85°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Warmth matters more than most floaters
  • Substrate — Not required. Feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also roots in pond margins
  • Propagation — Plantlets along trailing stems

Grower’s Notes

  • The leaf movement is real and repeatable. Touch, vibration or a sudden change in light causes the leaflets to fold within a second or two, reopening over the next few minutes. It is the same mechanism as the terrestrial sensitive plant.
  • Keep the foliage dry. Like other floaters, the leaves sit above the waterline and rot if constantly splashed — aim filter outflow below the surface.
  • It wants warmth. Growth slows markedly at the cool end of its range, so this is a poor choice for an unheated tank.
  • Propagate by separating plantlets that form along the trailing stems and floating them on. It spreads quickly enough to need thinning.
  • Expect folded leaves on arrival. Transit stress makes it close up; it reopens within a day of being floated in stable conditions.

Want to go deeper? Read our guide to the Best Floating Plants for Freshwater Aquariums.

Notes

  • Aquatic plants may experience minor cosmetic changes during shipping due to temperature, handling, and transit time. Leaves may temporarily fold or show slight stress but typically recover quickly once placed in suitable aquarium or pond conditions.

products.title: Bucephalandra Green Wavy Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Most Bucephalandra are bought for dark colour. Bucephalandra 'Green Wavy' is bought for shape — small, elongated leaves with a deep ruffle along the edge, in plain bright green. It clumps into miniature islands on wood and stone, and the wave gives texture where a dark Buce would just give shadow. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You'll Receive

  • One sealed 4-inch Vitro Culture® tissue culture bag
  • Approximately 4 small plantlets grown in sterile nutrient gel
  • 100% free from snails, algae, pesticides and pathogens
  • Rinse the gel away and separate the plantlets before planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Green Wavy Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Green Wavy'
  • Also known as — Buce, Bucep
  • Origin — Riverbanks of Borneo
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 2–4 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required, though it improves growth rate
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Green Buce solves a problem dark Buce creates. On dark wood, a deep-red or blue Bucephalandra disappears. Green Wavy stays visible — same slow, undemanding plant, but it reads as texture rather than a shadow.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Glue or tie it to rock or wood; buried rhizomes rot.
  • Growth is measured in months. That's why Buce holds its shape in a scape for years without trimming — and why patience after planting matters.
  • Some melting of older leaves after planting is normal as it converts to submerged growth. New leaves follow from the rhizome.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Bucephalandra Care Guide.

products.body_html:

  • Origin — North America and northern Europe
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Mature height — 1-3 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 65-75°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; this is a root feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower's Notes

  • Temperature is the deciding factor. This is a cool-water species. Held at 65-75°F it spreads steadily; run consistently warm, above the upper end, and it thins and stalls no matter what else is right. It suits an unheated or lightly heated tank far better than a tropical community.
  • Plant rosettes a few millimetres apart. Separate the culture into individual rosettes and set them close together. Each one throws runners outward, and tight initial spacing is what closes the carpet in months rather than a year.
  • Feed the substrate. Littorella is a root feeder with an unusually deep root system for its size. Aquasoil or root tabs under the planting area matter more than water column dosing.
  • Trim to keep it flat. Old leaves lengthen and lean over. Cutting the carpet back forces fresh short growth and stops the lower layer from being shaded out.
  • It is not Lilaeopsis. The two look nearly identical and are often confused, but they are unrelated plants from different families. Littorella prefers cooler water; care advice written for Lilaeopsis will not transfer cleanly.

products.title: Eleocharis Acicularis Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
The original hairgrass carpet. Eleocharis acicularis spreads by runners into a fine, needle-leaved lawn that stands 3–6 inches — taller and more flowing than the Mini form, so it reads as meadow grass rather than a close-cropped carpet. Dense enough that fry disappear into it. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® (tissue culture) format.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a Tissue Culture plants with vitamin liquid/gel
  • Bag size: Approx. 4 inches
  • Sustainable growth aquarium plants species
  • Tissue Culture Technology | 100% Free from Snail, Algae, Pathogen, and Bacteria plus Extended Shelf Life on all in Vitro Plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Dwarf Hairgrass
  • Scientific name — Eleocharis acicularis
  • Also known as — Needle Spikerush, Hairgrass
  • Origin — Widespread across the Northern Hemisphere
  • Placement — Foreground to low midground
  • Shipped size — 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag; blades short at arrival
  • Mature height — 3–6 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium. Light must reach the substrate, not just the surface
  • CO₂ — Recommended. It roughly halves the time to a closed carpet
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Taller than you may expect. Standard acicularis runs 3–6 inches and flows with the current. If you want a short, flat lawn instead, buy Eleocharis sp. Mini — the difference in final look is substantial.
  • Split the portion into small tufts and plant them half an inch apart. Planted as one mass it takes far longer to close.
  • Trim the carpet once. Cutting the blades back triggers a flush of new runners and thickens the mat.
  • Feed at the roots — runner production stalls without a nutrient substrate or root tabs.
  • Its height and density make it genuinely useful in breeding tanks, where fry need somewhere to vanish. Also available bare-root.

products.title: Bacopa Monnieri Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Bacopa monnieri is the stem plant that forgives everything. Thick, rounded, almost succulent leaves on an upright stem, no fussing over CO₂ or water chemistry, and it grows fast enough to fill a background quickly. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® version — many small plantlets, no snails, no algae.

What You'll Receive

  • Vitro Culture Bag (4-inch): Contains a generous cluster of young Bacopa monnieri plantlets, grown in a clean, sealed environment to ensure safe and easy introduction into your aquarium.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Moneywort
  • Scientific name — Bacopa monnieri
  • Also known as — Water Hyssop, Brahmi
  • Origin — Wetlands across the tropics, including India and the southern United States
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 inches
  • Mature height — 6-12 inches
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; also feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious stem
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • It is a genuine low-tech plant. Medium light and no CO₂ is enough. Tissue culture gives you a clean start; the plant itself asks for nothing beyond ordinary care.
  • Plant it shallow. The thick stem rots if pushed too deep. Bury the bottom node only, just enough to hold the stem upright, and roots come from that node within days.
  • Separate the culture before planting. Rinse the gel off and split the cluster into individual stems spaced half an inch apart. Planted as one lump the centre stems get shaded and drop their leaves.
  • Trim above a node and replant the top. Each cut stem branches into two below the cut, and the removed top roots readily. A single bag becomes a full background over a few trimming cycles.
  • It grows out of water too. Left to reach the surface it will emerge and produce small white flowers. Trim it below the waterline if you want it to stay submersed and bushy.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Bacopa Care Guide.

Notes

  • Color and density may vary depending on light, CO₂, and nutrients. Trim regularly to maintain shape and prevent excessive vertical growth. Avoid planting too deeply in substrate.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Hygrophila Pink Chai Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Want neon pink rather than red? Hygrophila lancea 'Pink Chai' carries vivid pink through its stems and narrow elongated leaves — a colour no other stem plant in our range produces. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format, free of snails, algae and pesticide residue.

What You’ll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing multiple Hygrophila Pink Chai plantlets, ready for rinsing, acclimation, and planting.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pink Chai
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila lancea 'Pink Chai'
  • Also known as — Hygrophila sp. 'Pink Chai', Hygrophila sp. 'Chai', Hygrophila Pink Lady
  • Origin — Natural hybrid of Hygrophila lancea 'Araguaia', found at South Island Aquarium in Singapore
  • Placement — Midground
  • Shipped size — Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 in
  • Mature height — 4–10 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium. Stronger light intensifies the pink
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5. Sensitive to sudden changes
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Stability matters more than intensity. Pink Chai reacts to sudden shifts in parameters more than most Hygrophila. A steady tank produces better colour than a heavily dosed one that swings.
  • Occasional stems revert. The hybrid is stable and cuttings normally come true pink, but a stem may sometimes return to the reddish-brown of the parent Hygrophila lancea 'Araguaia'. That is the hybrid behaving normally, not a mislabelled plant — remove reverted stems if you want the stand to stay uniformly pink.
  • Divide the cup into small clumps and plant them a little apart. Tissue culture stock establishes faster with space around it.
  • Rinse the gel off completely before planting or it clouds water and feeds algae in the first weeks.
  • Trim regularly and replant the tops. Topping forces branching, which is what turns a few stems into a block of colour.

Prefer rooted plants? See Hygrophila Pink Chai (Small Size) or the standard size.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Hygrophila Chai Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are sample representations. Actual colouration may vary depending on light intensity, CO₂, and nutrients. Growth form may differ during emersed-to-submerged transition.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Anubias Broad White Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Anubias Broad White carries some of the heaviest white variegation of any Anubias — wide leaves marbled cream and green, with individual leaves sometimes coming through almost entirely white. This is the tissue-culture format, which is the cheapest way into a plant that is otherwise expensive per rhizome.

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Anubias Broad White cultivated using Vitro Culture® tissue culture technology and sealed in sterile media for optimal quality and transport.

Pack Options Available:

1 Bag: One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing healthy Anubias Broad White plantlets.
5 Bags: Five 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bags containing healthy Anubias Broad White plantlets.
10 Bags: Ten 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bags containing healthy Anubias Broad White plantlets.

Each bag contains multiple young plantlets ready to rinse, separate, acclimate, and plant in your aquarium or high-humidity emersed setup.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Broad White Anubias
  • Scientific name — Anubias barteri 'Broad White'
  • Origin — Cultivated variety; the genus is native to West and Central Africa
  • Placement — Midground, attached to wood or stone
  • Mature height — 6-10 inches
  • Growth rate — Very slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light is the fastest way to lose this plant — see the note below.
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • White tissue has no chlorophyll, which is what makes this an advanced plant. A heavily variegated leaf produces far less energy than a green one, so growth is slower, damage takes longer to recover from, and algae gets a head start on the white areas. Keep it shaded and it will be fine; put it under a strong light and it will decline.
  • Rinse the gel off and separate the plantlets before mounting. Attach the rhizome to wood or stone — never bury it.
  • Tissue-culture plants start very small, and a very slow plant with reduced chlorophyll starts slower still. Give this one a season before judging it.
  • Variegation is unpredictable. Some leaves come mostly white, some mostly green. An all-white leaf will eventually exhaust itself and drop — that is normal, not a fault.
  • Sterile media means no snails, algae or pesticide residue, which is why this format suits shrimp tanks.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Anubias Care Guide.

Notes

Plants grown in tissue culture are produced in sterile laboratory environments and may appear smaller than mature aquarium plants. Once introduced into the aquarium with proper lighting and nutrients, they will gradually adapt and develop into fully established plants.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Echinodorus Pink Princess Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
A sword plant in pastel. Echinodorus 'Pink Princess' — also sold as Pink Amazon Sword — grows smooth lanceolate leaves in blush pink to soft rose rather than the usual green or burgundy, on a tidy upright rosette. This is the sterile tissue culture version.

What You'll Receive

  • Vitro Culture® Bag (4-inch): You will receive one sealed 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag containing approximately 4 small Pink Princess Sword plantlets, cultivated in a sterile lab environment. Simply rinse the nutrient gel under clean water, gently separate the plantlets, and plant them in your substrate.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pink Princess Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus 'Pink Princess'
  • Also known as — Pink Amazon Sword
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the genus is native to the Americas
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10-16 inches
  • Suits — 20 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — aquasoil or root tabs under the crown.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette; also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on aerial floral stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Plantlets arrive light green. Pink develops as the leaves mature under your own lighting, usually over the first month or two. A bag that looks plain green on day one is normal, not mislabelled.
  • Root tabs are what hold the pink. Swords feed almost entirely through their roots. Without a fertilised root zone the colour washes out and growth slows, no matter how bright the light is.
  • Never bury the crown. Cover the roots and leave the growing point at substrate level. A buried crown rots from the centre and does not recover.
  • Separate the plantlets before planting. Rinse the gel off and plant the four individually with space between them. Planted as a clump they shade each other and the inner ones fail.
  • Light intensity decides the shade of pink. Medium light gives a pale blush; stronger light deepens it toward rose. It is the one variable worth adjusting if the colour disappoints.

Two ways to buy this plant. This listing is the 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag — about four sterile plantlets, the cheapest way in and roughly a year of growing on. There is also an established plant, bare-root, bunched or potted, if you want colour this season.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Amazon Sword & Echinodorus Care Guide.

Notes

  • Coloration may vary based on lighting intensity, nutrients, and tank conditions. Younger plantlets may appear light green and gradually develop pink tones as they mature. Avoid burying the crown during planting.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

Its vibrant pink to reddish coloration and exceptional leaf structure make it a fantastic addition to any aquarium.

products.title: Rotala Sunset
products.body_html:
Rounder leaves, warmer colour. Rotala sp. 'Sunset' shifts from green through orange-red into purple depending on light and feeding — and the quickest way to tell it from its close relative Rotala ramosior 'Florida' is leaf shape: Sunset's leaves are noticeably rounder, Florida's more pointed.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Rotala Sunset
  • Scientific name — Rotala sp. 'Sunset'
  • Also known as — Rotala ramosior 'Sunset'
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — High. Light intensity sets how far it moves from green toward orange
  • CO₂ — Recommended

  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient substrate or root tabs

products.title: Bacopa Salzmannii
products.body_html:
A colour-shifting stem plant with rounded, slightly elliptical leaves. Grown emersed it is green; once submerged it moves through light orange to pink and purple, and how far it goes depends on your light and nutrients.

products.title: Cuphea Anagalloidea
products.body_html:
Cuphea anagalloidea is a delicate small stem plant that requires a lot of care.
The brilliant shade of scarlet that may be found on the upper surface of the submerged leaves is brought out to its fullest potential when exposed to bright light. This plant was initially introduced into the aquarium hobby under the name Rotala sp. Araguaia; however, it was later determined that it belongs to the Cuphea species. Cuphea Anagalloidea can only grow vertically. It looks best when used in a group in the middleground as a color accent. The upper edges of the leaves turn a bright crimson to orange-red color under high lighting, but the stem remains green. Sufficient lighting, with plenty CO2 and nutrients, and soft water are all recommended.

products.title: Bucephalandra Giant Velvet
products.body_html:
Matte, not glossy. Bucephalandra sp. 'Giant Velvet' has a soft velvet surface on broad dark green leaves — it absorbs light where most Buce reflect it, giving depth rather than shine. "Giant" is relative: at 4–6 inches it is large for a Bucephalandra, where most of the genus sits at 2–3.

What You’ll Receive

  • Bunched plants | Bucephalandra plants with foam, and lead weight

  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Giant Velvet'
  • Also known as — Buce, Bucep
  • Origin — Borneo
  • Placement — Midground, on wood or stone

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner

products.title: Bucephalandra Theia Green
products.body_html:
Theia Green is the Bucephalandra for people who do not want blue or purple. Vivid green leaves with a wavy edge and a glossy surface, growing in a compact bushy clump — and like every Buce, it wants attaching to hardscape rather than planting.

Choose the format that best suits your aquascaping needs and create a vibrant, lush underwater environment with our premium aquatic plants.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Theia Green Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Theia Green'
  • Also known as — Buce, Bucep; tribe Schismatoglottideae, family Araceae

  • Expect roughly an inch of growth per year. Buce is among the slowest plants sold. Most arrive around 2-3 inches and stay close to that for a long time, which is exactly why it holds a scape's composition without trimming.
  • Never bury the rhizome. The horizontal stem must sit in open water, tied or glued to a surface. Buried, it rots — and at this growth rate the loss is not recoverable in a season.

products.title: Bucephalandra Lalina
products.body_html:
Lalina carries subtle ripples across a deep green to bluish leaf, with a soft metallic sheen that shows under moderate light. It is one of the quieter iridescent varieties — texture first, shimmer second.

What You'll Receive

Enhance your aquarium with our fresh, high-quality plants, available in convenient formats:

  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 1-2 plants bundled with a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 1-2 plants potted in rockwool and a net pot for secure growth and easy placement.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Lalina Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Lalina'
  • Also known as — Buce, Bucep
  • Origin — Borneo (genus range)
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Too much light brings algae the plant is too slow to outgrow.
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5

products.title: Ceratopteris Siliquosa
products.body_html:
Want a fast plant that propagates itself? Water Sprite grows fine, lacy fern foliage that fills a background in weeks — planted or floating, your choice — and produces new plants along its own leaf margins with no effort from you.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as Fresh-cut Plants, Bunched Plants or Potted Plants:

  • Fresh-cut Plants: Approximately 6 loose fresh-cut plants without root.
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 6 fresh-cut plants without root bundled with a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 6 fresh-cut plants without root potted in rockwool and a net pot for secure growth and easy placement.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Water Sprite, Narrow Leaf Water Sprite
  • Scientific name — Ceratopteris thalictroides 'Siliquosa'
  • Placement — Midground to background, or floating
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Feeds mainly from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Plantlets on leaf margins

Grower’s Notes

  • It clones itself along its leaves. Small plantlets form on the leaf edges and on older leaves as they age. Once one has a few fronds and roots, detach it and plant or float it — this is how a single portion becomes a tankful without you doing anything.
  • Planted or floating are both correct. Floating it grows faster and shades the tank below; planted it grows more upright. Floating is the usual choice in fry and shrimp tanks.
  • It strips nitrate quickly, which makes it genuinely useful in a new or heavily stocked tank rather than just decorative.
  • Roots are fragile when planted. Bury only enough to hold it and let it anchor itself, or it tears loose.

Water Sprite is not Water Wisteria. This is a true fern, growing as a rosette and reproducing from leaf plantlets. Water Wisteria is Hygrophila difformis — a flowering stem plant with paired leaves up an upright stem. Both have finely divided foliage, which is where the confusion starts.

products.title: Ludwigia Meta
products.body_html:
Ludwigia Meta is what people reach for when Ludwigia Pantanal has beaten them. It gives the same fine whorls of narrow leaves and the same orange-to-red burn under strong light, but without Pantanal's intolerance for anything less than perfect. Still uncommon in the trade, and still a centrepiece plant.

What You'll Receive

Choose the format that suits your aquascaping needs:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 6+ unrooted stems
  • Bunched Plants: 6+ fresh-cut stems without root, bundled with foam and plant weight
  • Potted Plants: 6+ fresh-cut stems potted in rockwool within a 2-inch net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ludwigia Meta
  • Scientific name — Ludwigia inclinata var. verticillata 'Meta'
  • Also known as — Ludwigia sp. 'Meta'
  • Origin — Departamento del Meta, central Colombia
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 6-14 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.0. Soft water, carbonate hardness below 4°dH
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs, plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious stem, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • It arrives green and it is supposed to. Our stock is grown emersed, where the leaves are plain green. Orange and red develop only after the plant converts to submersed growth under your lighting — usually three to four weeks in.
  • Soft water matters more than light. Meta colours and grows best with carbonate hardness under 4°dH. In hard water it stays green and slowly stalls no matter how much light and iron you throw at it — test KH rather than chasing a pH number.
  • Easier than Pantanal, same look. If you have lost Ludwigia Pantanal to melt or stunting, Meta gives a similar fine-leaved red without the same intolerance of imperfect conditions.
  • It branches poorly, so plant more stems. Meta grows straight up with little side-shooting. Density comes from planting a group close together, not from waiting for one stem to bush out.
  • Replant the tops, discard the bases. As with most fine-leaved Ludwigia, the lower stem goes bare with age. Cut the top few inches, replant them, and pull the old base.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Ludwigia Care Guide.

Notes

  • Ludwigia Meta ships in its emersed green form. Once submerged and provided with strong light and nutrients, it will gradually develop its iconic orange to red hues. Slight leaf melt during transition is normal.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Ludwigia sp. White
products.body_html:
Want white foliage rather than red? Ludwigia inclinata var. verticillata 'White' produces slender leaves in pale pink through near-white — a colour almost nothing else in a planted tank offers. It is also one of the most demanding stem plants we sell, and worth understanding before you buy.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as loose Fresh-cut plants, Bunched plants, or Potted plants
  • Fresh-cut plants | Approx. 6 stems, loose fresh-cut stems without root
  • Bunched plants | Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems without root, bundled with foam, and lead weight
  • Potted plants | Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems without root, potted with net pot and rockwool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ludwigia White
  • Scientific name — Ludwigia inclinata var. verticillata 'White'
  • Also known as — Ludwigia sp. White, Ludwigia sp. Pink
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Central and South America
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems, roughly 4-8 in
  • Mature height — 6–14 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High. Non-negotiable for the white and pink colouring
  • CO₂ — Required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient soil, root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Leaf form changes completely between emersed and submersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • The pale colour is why it is difficult. White and pale pink tissue carries very little chlorophyll, so the plant photosynthesises inefficiently and has far less margin than a green or even a red Ludwigia. High light and stable CO₂ are not optional extras here — they are what keep it alive.
  • Stability matters more than any single value. It reacts badly to swinging CO₂ or a large water change, and typically responds by melting from the lower stem upward.
  • Handle it by the base only. The fine whorled leaves strip where you grip, and bare nodes do not refoliate.
  • Trim and replant the tops. Lower sections rarely recover well enough to be worth keeping on a plant this slow to build.
  • It arrives green or greenish. The pink and white develop only once it has converted to submersed growth under strong light — judge the colour after a few weeks.

  • Common name — Aragon Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Aragon'
  • Also known as — Buce, Bucep; tribe Schismatoglottideae, family Araceae
  • Origin — Borneo, Indonesia

  • Light — Low to medium

  • Expect roughly an inch of growth per year. Bucephalandra is among the slowest plants sold. Most arrive around 2-3 inches and stay close to that for a long time — which is exactly why it holds a scape's composition without trimming.

products.body_html:
The bluest Buce we stock. Bucephalandra sp. 'Super Blue' carries an unusually strong blue sheen across dark leaves — more pronounced than the faint iridescence most of the genus shows. products.body_html:

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Too much light brings algae the plant is too slow to outgrow.

  • A plain green Buce is the easiest one to keep alive. Iridescent and coloured varieties disappoint when the light is wrong; this one looks the same in every corner of the tank, which makes it the sensible choice for a first Bucephalandra.

  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.
  • Give it flow. Bucephalandra are rheophytes from fast Borneo streams, and moderate current keeps the leaves clean of debris and algae.

products.title: Echinodorus Aflame Vitro Culture (Purple Knight Sword)
products.body_html:
Echinodorus 'Aflame' is a sword plant that skips the green stage. New leaves emerge burgundy and darken toward purple-black as they harden, held in an upright rosette rather than the sprawling form most swords take. It gives a planted tank a red centrepiece without a single stem plant.

What You'll Receive

  • You will receive one sealed 4-inch Vitro Culture bag containing approximately 3–4 young Echinodorus Aflame plantlets

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Purple Knight Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus 'Aflame'
  • Also known as — Aflame Sword
  • Origin — Cultivated hybrid; parent species from South America
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10-16 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; this is a root feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on flower stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Root tabs are what produce the colour. Swords take nearly all their nutrition from the substrate. Water column dosing alone gives you a pale, slow Aflame; a fertilised root zone gives you the burgundy the plant is bought for.
  • Never bury the crown. The growing point at the centre of the rosette must sit at substrate level. Covered, it rots — the leaves go first and the plant does not come back.
  • Plantlets arrive green. Tissue culture stock is grown under conditions that favour growth over pigment. Red and purple develop as the plant establishes under your lighting, usually over the first month or two.
  • It propagates from flower stalks, not runners. A mature Aflame sends up an inflorescence that produces daughter plants along its length. Let each grow roots and two or three leaves before cutting it free.

products.title: Nymphaea Georgia Peach | Pink Hardy Water Lily
products.body_html:
Soft peach-pink, and hardy. Nymphaea 'Georgia Peach' is a hardy water lily with gentle peach-pink blooms that float at the surface among classic lily pads. The colour is quieter than the hot pinks and reds — it reads as elegant rather than loud, and it settles into a planted pond instead of fighting with it.

What You'll Receive

Choose the pack size that fits your pond:

  • 1 Tuber
  • 5 Tubers

Each tuber sent is healthy, young, and includes approximately 1–2 new sprouting leaves, carefully selected and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory® to ensure strong establishment.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Georgia Peach Water Lily
  • Scientific name — Nymphaea 'Georgia Peach'
  • Type — Hardy water lily
  • Flower — Peach-pink, opening at the water surface
  • Foliage — Classic rounded floating pads
  • Placement — Outdoor ponds and water gardens; centrepiece

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Sunlight — Full sun; required for consistent flowering
  • Water — Cool to moderate temperatures
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich aquatic soil or clay-based substrate in a wide, shallow pot
  • Planting angle — Hardy rhizome: 45°, growing tip up, at the pot edge pointing toward the centre
  • Overwintering — Hardy. Stays in the pond year-round; move the pot below the freeze line in autumn
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Peach is a hard colour to find in a hardy lily. Most of the range runs pink, red, white or yellow. If you want something softer that still overwinters outdoors, the choices are few and this is one of the better ones.
  • Blooms sit at the surface rather than standing above it, which gives the classic lily-pad look people picture when they imagine a pond.
  • Hardy, so no lifting and no indoor storage. Cut back the foliage in autumn and move the pot deeper.
  • Full sun is the deciding factor for flowering. In part shade you get pads and few blooms.
  • The pad cover shades the water, which limits algae and gives fish somewhere to hide.

New to planting water lilies? Read our complete Water Lily Planting Guide — tuber angle, soil, depth and the one mistake that kills most first lilies.

products.body_html:

Select the quantity that best fits your aquascape needs using the variant options above.

  • 1 Bag Option:
    You will receive one (1) 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag, yielding approximately 3–4 healthy clump plants of Lilaeopsis brasiliensis.
  • 5 Bags Option:
    You will receive five (5) individual 4-inch Vitro Culture® bags, each yielding approximately 3–4 healthy clump plants.

Each bag is grown in sterile Vitro Culture® conditions and is free from algae, snails, and pests. Plantlets are ready to rinse, divide, and plant directly into nutrient-rich substrate.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Micro Sword, also known as Brazilian Micro Sword
  • Scientific name — Lilaeopsis brasiliensis
  • Origin — South America
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Mature height — 1–3 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Light reaching the substrate is what makes it carpet
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required. It carpets faster and denser with it
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Fine, nutrient-rich substrate — root feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Divide the cup into many small clumps. Plant them an inch apart and let the runners close the gaps. Planted as one mass it takes months longer, because runners only travel into open substrate.
  • Root tabs decide the outcome. In inert gravel Micro Sword survives but never thickens — the most common reason a carpet stalls.
  • Use fine substrate. Its roots are short and delicate and cannot grip coarse gravel, so clumps float free before they anchor.
  • Rinse the gel off completely before planting or it clouds water and feeds algae in the first weeks.
  • It is slow to start. Expect little visible progress for the first month while it roots, then steady spread.

Despite the name, this is not a sword plant. Lilaeopsis is unrelated to Echinodorus (Amazon Swords) or Helanthium (chain swords) — it stays small and carpets, where true swords grow large or spread as rosettes.

  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Buy it for texture, not colour. It stays green. What it contributes is a fine, feathered silhouette next to swords, Anubias or Cryptocoryne — contrast built from leaf shape rather than pigment.
  • It's slower and fussier than the common Bacopa species. Steady light and stable water matter more here than they do for Bacopa caroliniana or monnieri.
  • Trim and replant tops repeatedly to build density; single stems look sparse.
  • Fine leaves collect detritus in low-flow corners. Give it moderate water movement or it looks dusty.
  • Some leaf drop after planting is the emersed-to-submerged conversion, not a problem to fix.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Bacopa Care Guide.

Notes

  • Some initial leaf drop or melting may occur as the plant transitions from emersed to submerged growth. This is normal, and healthy new submerged growth will follow with proper care.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.body_html:
Purple is rarer than red in a planted tank. Rotala ramosior 'Florida' is one of the few stem plants that gets there — lavender through to deep violet under strong light and CO₂, on upright stems with narrow leaves in opposite pairs. Native to North America, and still uncommon in the hobby.

products.title: Hygrophila corymbosa 'Cherry Leaf'
products.body_html:
Most red background plants want CO₂, strong light and a dosing routine before they show any colour. Hygrophila corymbosa 'Cherry Leaf' is a Hygrophila — fast, hardy, forgiving — that happens to come in cherry pink and red. That combination is unusual at this size.

  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Background
  • Mature height — 10-20 inches

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner

Grower's Notes

  • The colour sits on the top leaves. Cherry pink develops on new growth nearest the light; lower leaves stay green. Trimming and replanting the tops is what keeps a stand looking red rather than green with a red fringe.
  • Iron, not light alone. Under medium light with steady micronutrient dosing the tops flush cherry. Strong light without iron gives you a fast green Hygrophila instead.
  • It is fast, so plan on trimming. Ten to twenty inches arrives quickly. Topping the stems and replanting the cuttings keeps the group at the height you want and doubles your plant count each time.
  • Beginner difficulty is genuine here. Unlike most red plants this is a hardy Hygrophila underneath. It will grow in a low-tech tank — you simply get less colour without dosing.
  • Plant the stems apart. Bunched stems rot where the foam and weight sit. Separate them and space each half an inch apart so light reaches the lower nodes.

products.title: Hyptis Lorentziana (Purple Mint)
products.body_html:
Hyptis lorentziana is an aquarium mint. Deep purple-red leaves in opposite pairs on square stems, from a genus better known for culinary herbs than for aquascapes — and still uncommon enough that most people have never seen it in a tank.

What You'll Receive

Enhance your aquarium with our versatile selection of high-quality aquatic plants, available in three convenient formats:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Includes approximately 3+ loose, fresh-cut stems without roots. Perfect for flexible planting arrangements.
  • Fresh-Cut Bunched: Approximately 3+ fresh-cut stems without roots, bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Fresh-Cut Potted: About 3+ fresh-cut stems without roots, securely potted in a net pot with rockwool, ensuring stability and healthy growth.

Choose the format that best suits your aquascaping needs and create a vibrant, lush underwater environment with our premium aquatic plants.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Purple Mint
  • Scientific name — Hyptis lorentziana
  • Also known as — formerly circulated as "Hemigraphis traian"
  • Family — Lamiaceae, the mint family
  • Origin — South America
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 6-14 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-78°F, pH 6.0-7.0
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs, plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious stem
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • It was misidentified for years. The plant circulated in the hobby as "Hemigraphis traian" until 2009, when it was correctly placed in Hyptis, in the mint family. Old care advice written under the wrong name is still floating around — worth knowing if you search for it.
  • Cut above a leaf pair, not mid-stem. Trim roughly three to four inches above the substrate, directly above a pair of leaves. That is what triggers the lateral shoots that turn one stem into a bush.
  • Strong light holds the purple. Under medium light it leans green-bronze. The deep purple-red the plant is bought for needs intensity plus consistent iron dosing.
  • It gets big in the wild and stays manageable in a tank. Emersed at a pond margin it reaches two metres; submersed and trimmed it stays in the 6-14 inch range.
  • Plant stems individually. Square-stemmed plants rot readily where a bunching band sits. Separate them and space each half an inch apart.

products.title: Vallisneria nana 'Striped'
products.body_html:
Want pattern on a narrow-leaved Val? Vallisneria nana 'Striped' — also sold as Tiger Val — carries brown striping and speckling along slim green blades. It gives you markings and movement without the solid curtain a broad-leaved Vallisneria creates.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as loose bare-root plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Bare-root Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual loose, bare-root plants
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Striped Vallisneria Nana, also known as Tiger Vallisneria
  • Scientific name — Vallisneria nana 'Striped'
  • Also known as — Vallisneria nana 'Tiger'
  • Placement — Background
  • Mature height — 20–30 in
  • Leaf width — Narrow, though noticeably wider than standard nana
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–8.0. Tolerates hard, alkaline water well
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • It stays green under strong light. This is the practical difference from Vallisneria spiralis 'Leopard', which develops red tones and heavier marbling under intensity. Striped keeps its green base with brown tiger markings whatever you throw at it.
  • Striping varies plant to plant, and some leaves carry more than others. That is normal for this cultivar rather than a sign of a poor specimen.
  • Plant the crown at the substrate line, never below it. A buried crown rots — the usual reason a new Val fails in the first fortnight.
  • Feed at the roots. In inert gravel it survives but barely spreads; root tabs are what turn three plants into a stand.
  • Don't trim the tops to control height. Cut Val leaves brown at the cut and stay that way — remove whole leaves at the base instead.

Want the finest blade instead? Standard Vallisneria nana is the narrowest in the genus at roughly 1 mm, without the markings.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Vallisneria Care Guide.

Notes

  • Some leaf melting may occur when transitioning to a new tank. Stripe intensity and patterning may vary between individual plants. Provide stable lighting and substrate for best performance.
  • Some aquatic plants are restricted in certain U.S. states — check before ordering, and never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Hygrophila Corymbosa
products.body_html:
Big leaves, fast. Hygrophila corymbosa — Giant Hygro or Temple Plant — grows broad, bright green leaves on sturdy upright stems and reaches 10–20 inches quickly without CO₂. Where fine-leaved stems give texture, this gives mass, which is exactly what a bare background needs.

  • Fresh-cut Bunched | approx. 5 fresh-cut plants bundle with foam, and lead weight
  • Fresh-cut Potted | approx. 5 fresh-cut plants potted with net pot and rock wool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Corymbosa, Giant Hygro, Temple Plant
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila corymbosa
  • Also known as — Nomaphila corymbosa, Hygrophila stricta
  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 5 fresh-cut stems, roughly 4-8 in
  • Mature height — 10–20 in
  • Suits — 20 gallons and up

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient substrate or root tabs recommended
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Leaf size is the reason to choose it. Most fast background stems are fine-leaved. Corymbosa's broad leaves read as solid green from a distance, which is why Dutch-style layouts use it to build depth against narrow-leaved neighbours.
  • It will outgrow the tank if you let it. Trim every few weeks or it reaches the surface and shades everything in front.
  • Trim above a leaf node and replant the tops — cuttings root within days.
  • Lower leaves yellowing usually means the group is planted too densely. Space stems an inch or more apart.
  • Fast growth makes it a useful nutrient sponge while a new tank settles and slower plants establish.
  • The narrow-leaved Hygro Willow is the same genus with a completely different silhouette, and the compact 'Kompakt' form stays under 8 inches for smaller tanks.

products.body_html:
Want a Hygrophila that stays in the midground? Hygrophila corymbosa 'Kompakt' is the dwarf cultivar — broad bright green oval leaves on stems with much shorter internodes, so it grows into a dense low bush instead of running for the surface like standard corymbosa.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Kompakt, also known as Compact Hygrophila
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila corymbosa 'Kompakt'
  • Also known as — Nomaphila siamensis 'Parvifolia'
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Midground
  • Shipped size — Approx. 3+ fresh-cut stems, roughly 3-6 in
  • Mature height — 4–8 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium. Stronger light keeps the internodes short and the bush tight
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed in paludariums
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops and side shoots

Grower’s Notes

  • Short internodes are the whole point. Standard Hygrophila corymbosa stretches to 20 inches and beyond with wide gaps between leaf pairs. 'Kompakt' packs them close, which is why it holds a hedge shape where the parent plant does not — and why it fits a 10-gallon tank that the parent would swamp.
  • Light keeps it compact. Under weak light the internodes lengthen and it loses the dwarf habit — trimming won't bring it back.
  • Trim and replant the tops. Each cut forces side shoots, which is how a few stems become a solid midground block.
  • Root tabs help noticeably. It draws from both roots and water column, and leaf size drops in inert gravel.

products.title: Cameroon Moss
products.body_html:
Leaves big enough to see. Cameroon Moss from West Africa grows overlapping rounded leaves along creeping stems, forming a dense cushion rather than a fine haze — which is why it also travels under the name Giant Pearl Moss. Attach it to wood or stone and it builds a thick green mat.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a small portion, loose moss
  • Approx. 2" x 2" / 5cm x 5cm portion

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Cameroon Moss
  • Scientific name — Vesicularia sp. 'Cameroon'
  • Also known as — Giant Pearl Moss, Plagiochilaceae sp. Cameroon
  • Origin — Cameroon, West Africa
  • Placement — Midground, attached to driftwood, stone or décor
  • Mature height — 2–4 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Strong light brings algae into the cushion
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Fragmentation — divide and re-attach

Grower’s Notes

  • Leaf size is what you're buying. Java and Christmas Moss read as texture; Cameroon's larger overlapping leaves stay legible up close, which makes it worth placing at the front where it will actually be seen.
  • Tie it thinly and let it thicken. A dense pad traps detritus and rots from underneath.
  • It absorbs nutrients straight from the water column, so liquid dosing does more here than anything in the substrate.
  • Slow growth means it holds a shape for months — but also that algae, once in it, is very hard to clear.
  • It works well as a spawning surface for egg-scattering fish and as shrimp grazing ground.

products.title: Mini Christmas Moss
products.body_html:
Want the Christmas Moss shape at nano scale? Mini Christmas Moss branches into the same triangular fir-tree fronds as the standard form, at roughly half the size — which means the pattern stays visible on small hardscape instead of reading as a green blur.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as small, loose portion
  • Approx. 2 inches in size

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Mini Christmas Moss, also known as Mini Xmas Moss
  • Scientific name — Vesicularia montagnei 'Mini'
  • Also known as — Taxiphyllum sp. 'Mini Christmas', Vesicularia sp. 'Mini Christmas'
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. High light grows algae, not moss
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5. Cooler water gives tighter branching
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Fragmentation

Grower’s Notes

  • Cooler water keeps the shape. Like standard Christmas Moss, the tight triangular branching is a cool-water trait. In a warm tank it grows looser and longer and starts to look like ordinary Java Moss — the small size makes that loss more obvious, not less.
  • Attach a thin layer, not a thick pad. A dense clump rots underneath where no light or flow reaches, and the whole piece lets go.
  • Trim regularly. Each cut forces branching, which is what keeps the fir-tree structure crisp rather than stringy.
  • Never bury it in substrate, and never let algae establish — there is no safe way to remove algae from moss.

Want the full-size version? See standard Christmas Moss.
